title: Weighing Your Options
objectives: I can name the steps of a hard decision using ten precise words.
I can tell the difference between deliberate as a verb and as an adjective.
I can use criteria to explain why one option is better than another.
I can write a short plan that names an obstacle and a strategy to overcome it.
rationale: Sixth graders face real choices and are asked to explain choices in stories, history, and science. These ten words name each step in a decision: the hard moment (dilemma), the options (alternative), what matters (priority, criteria), the thinking (deliberate, eliminate), the plan (strategy, implement), and the resistance (obstacle, overcome). Students who can name the steps can describe a decision rather than only report what happened, and the same vocabulary supports cause-and-effect writing, problem-solution texts, and argument.

words.def: A hard choice between two options, where each one has a cost.
words.ex: Lila faced a dilemma: tell the teacher about the broken window or let her friend take the blame.
words.ex2: The town faced a dilemma because the only route for a new road ran through the old forest.
words.nonExample: Picking between two flavors of ice cream you love is a pleasant choice, not a dilemma.
words.rel: a choice with no easy answer

apps.academic: Characters in stories often face a dilemma that shows who they really are.
apps.spoken: I'm in a dilemma: I can't be at the game and the recital at the same time.
apps.writing: Use dilemma only for hard choices where every option costs something.

cloze.s: Maya's ___ was that she had promised to babysit and to play in the championship game, both at noon.

cloze2.s: The captain faced a ___: rest her tired star player or risk losing the game.

misuse.s: It was an easy dilemma, because one choice was clearly perfect and the other was clearly terrible.
misuse.why: A dilemma is a hard choice where both options cost something; an obvious best choice is not a dilemma.

visual.alt: A thinking face above a balance scale holding two equal weights.

words.frame: My dilemma was whether to ___ or to ___.

words.def: Another choice or way of doing something that you could pick instead.
words.ex: If the bus is late, an alternative is to ride our bikes to school.
words.ex2: The cafeteria offered a vegetarian alternative to every meat dish on the menu.
words.nonExample: Doing exactly the same thing again is not an alternative.

apps.academic: A strong problem-solution essay compares the best plan with at least one alternative.
apps.spoken: That road is closed, so we need an alternative.
apps.writing: Use alternative as a noun for the other choice; use alternatively to introduce it.

cloze.s: The game was canceled because of rain, so the coach suggested an indoor ___: a trivia night.

cloze2.s: When the printer broke, Kai's ___ was to copy the notes by hand.

misuse.s: The only choice available was a true alternative, because nothing else could be picked.
misuse.why: An alternative is another choice you could pick; if there is only one option, there is no alternative.

visual.alt: A railroad track that splits into two routes.

words.frame: Instead of ___, a good alternative is ___.

words.def: Something that matters most and should be dealt with first.
words.ex: Finishing the science report is my top priority this weekend.
words.ex2: The nurse made the sickest patient her first priority.
words.nonExample: A chore you plan to get to someday, if you feel like it, is not a priority.

apps.academic: A city budget shows a government's priorities by what it pays for first.
apps.spoken: My priority right now is getting enough sleep.
apps.writing: Use priority to show which goal a character puts ahead of the others.

cloze.s: Her first ___ after the flight landed was to call her parents and say she was safe.

cloze2.s: With only an hour left, the editors made fixing the front page their top ___.

misuse.s: Her top priority was the task she cared about least, so she left it at the bottom of her list.
misuse.why: A priority is what matters most and comes first, not what is last on the list.

visual.alt: A checklist with a star beside the first item.

words.def: Something that blocks your way or makes it harder to reach a goal.
words.ex: A fallen tree was the biggest obstacle on the hiking trail.
words.ex2: Fear of failing can be a bigger obstacle than the task itself.
words.nonExample: A clear, empty road is not an obstacle.

apps.academic: Many biographies describe the obstacles a person faced before reaching a goal.
apps.spoken: The only obstacle is getting a ride there.
apps.writing: Name the obstacle in a story so the reader can watch the character work around it.

cloze.s: The wall of thorny bushes was the first ___ the dog had to get past to reach the open field.

cloze2.s: Not having a quiet place to study was an ___ for Dev, so he started going to the library.

misuse.s: The open door was a major obstacle, so nobody could walk through it.
misuse.why: An obstacle blocks the way; an open door lets people through.

visual.alt: A runner approaching a barrier on a track.

words.def: A careful plan for reaching a goal, often made of several steps.
words.ex: The team's strategy was to pass quickly and shoot only when the goalie was out of position.
words.ex2: One good study strategy is to quiz yourself instead of rereading the chapter.
words.nonExample: Doing the first thing that comes to mind is not a strategy.

apps.academic: Reading strategies include predicting, summarizing, and rereading a hard sentence.
apps.spoken: What's your strategy for the math test?
apps.writing: Use strategy for a plan with several steps, not for a single action.

cloze.s: The chess club's ___ for the tournament was to protect the queen early and attack late.

cloze2.s: Our ___ for finishing the project on time was to divide the work into daily goals.

misuse.s: Their strategy was to have no plan at all and simply see what happened.
misuse.why: A strategy is a careful plan; having no plan is not a strategy.

visual.alt: A chess pawn beside a brain.

words.def: To think about something slowly and carefully before deciding.

senses.def: Done on purpose, not by accident.
senses.example: Her deliberate pause made the whole audience lean forward.

words.ex: The jury deliberated for two days before reaching a verdict.
words.ex2: Before choosing a middle school, Ana and her parents deliberated over every option.
words.nonExample: Pointing at the first item on a menu without reading it is not deliberating.

apps.academic: In history class, we read how a committee deliberated before writing its report.
apps.spoken: Give me a minute to deliberate.
apps.writing: The verb ends in a long a sound; the adjective meaning on purpose ends in a short i sound.

cloze.s: The council will ___ for hours before voting on the new park rules.

cloze2.s: Don't rush into it; take a few minutes to ___ about which route is the safest.

misuse.s: The jury deliberated for one second and gave its verdict without any discussion.
misuse.why: To deliberate is to think slowly and carefully; one second with no discussion is rushing.

visual.alt: A thought bubble beside an hourglass.

words.frame: Before making a big choice, I deliberate by ___.

words.def: To remove something completely, or to rule an option out.
words.ex: Mr. Cruz eliminated two choices on the quiz that he knew were wrong.
words.ex2: The new recycling program helped the school eliminate plastic cups from the cafeteria.
words.nonExample: Moving a wrong answer to a different spot on the page does not eliminate it.

apps.academic: On multiple-choice tests, eliminating wrong answers raises your chances of choosing the right one.
apps.spoken: Let's eliminate the ideas that cost too much.
apps.writing: Use eliminate for removing a thing completely or ruling out a possibility.

cloze.s: The detective began to ___ suspects whose alibis could be proven by witnesses.

cloze2.s: By crossing out answers she knew were false, Hana was able to ___ two of the four choices.

misuse.s: To eliminate a wrong answer, Ravi circled it and kept it as his final choice.
misuse.why: To eliminate is to remove or rule out; keeping the answer as a final choice is the opposite.

visual.alt: A red X crossed over one choice on a written list.

words.def: To put a plan, rule, or idea into action.
words.ex: The school will implement the new recycling plan in January.
words.ex2: It is easy to write a schedule, but harder to implement it every single day.
words.nonExample: Writing a plan and filing it in a drawer is not implementing it.

apps.academic: Governments implement laws by creating offices and rules that make them work.
apps.spoken: We voted yesterday, and we start to implement the plan tomorrow.
apps.writing: Use implement for acting on a plan, rule, or idea, not for a physical task.

cloze.s: The city plans to ___ the new bike lanes next summer, once the paint arrives.

cloze2.s: After the class voted on the seating chart, the teacher began to ___ it on Monday morning.

misuse.s: The mayor implemented the plan by never doing anything it said.
misuse.why: To implement is to put a plan into action; ignoring it is the opposite.

visual.alt: A wrench resting on a written plan.

words.frame: To implement our plan, we will first ___.

words.def: To succeed in dealing with a problem or fear that stood in your way.
words.ex: Sam overcame his fear of deep water by taking swimming lessons every week.
words.ex2: The small town overcame the loss of its factory by opening a farmers' market.
words.nonExample: Turning back at the first hard step is not overcoming a problem.

apps.academic: Biographies often show how a person overcame hardship to reach a goal.
apps.spoken: She overcame her nervousness once she started talking.
apps.writing: Use overcome with the thing that was in the way: overcome a fear, an injury, a delay.

cloze.s: With daily practice, Marta hoped to ___ her fear of speaking in front of the class.

cloze2.s: The hikers had to ___ icy winds and a steep slope to reach the summit.

misuse.s: She overcame her shyness by hiding in her room whenever visitors came.
misuse.why: To overcome a problem is to get past it; hiding from it leaves the shyness in charge.

visual.alt: A strong arm raised in front of a mountain peak.

words.def: The standards or rules used to judge something or make a choice.
words.ex: The judges' criteria included originality, neatness, and how clearly the project was explained.
words.ex2: Our criteria for a class pet were that it had to be quiet, safe, and cheap to feed.
words.nonExample: Flipping a coin to decide uses no criteria at all.
words.rel: the rules for judging a choice

apps.academic: A rubric lists the criteria a teacher will use to score your work.
apps.spoken: What criteria are we using to pick the winner?
apps.writing: Criteria is plural; the singular is criterion. Write 'the criteria are', not 'the criteria is'.

cloze.s: The ___ for joining the chess team are simple: you must know the rules and come to practice.

cloze2.s: Using clear ___ such as cost, safety, and size, the committee ranked the three bus designs.

misuse.s: The judges had no criteria, but they scored every project using the same written standards.
misuse.why: Criteria are the standards used to judge; scoring by the same written standards means they did have criteria.

visual.alt: A checklist next to a ruler.

passage.title: The Saturday Problem
paras: Marcus stared at the two flyers on his desk. The regional soccer tournament and the state science fair were on the same Saturday. His team needed him in goal, but his volcano model had finally earned a place at the fair. It was a real dilemma: whichever choice he made, he would let someone down.

His older sister Alba suggested a method. "Write down every alternative," she said, "even the silly ones." Marcus listed four: skip the tournament, skip the fair, ask the fair for an early time slot, or find a way to do both. Alba asked what mattered most. After he deliberated for a whole evening, Marcus named his priority: not letting either group down.

Next they wrote criteria for a good solution. It had to keep both promises, it had to be possible before Saturday, and it could not cost his parents extra money. Skipping either event broke the first rule, so they eliminated those two alternatives. Two options were left.

The plan became a strategy with two steps. First, Marcus emailed the judges and asked for the earliest slot. Second, his coach agreed to start him in the second half. One obstacle remained: the fair was across town, and the game began forty minutes after the judging ended. Alba found a bus route that would arrive with five minutes to spare.

On Saturday, Marcus implemented the plan step by step. The judges praised his volcano, he sprinted to the bus, and he reached the field in time for the second half. His team won by one goal. Marcus knew he had overcome the problem not by luck, but by thinking before he acted.

choices: a mistake that cannot be fixed
a hard choice in which each option has a cost
a plan made long ago
a quarrel with a sister
qs.why: Marcus must pick between two events, and either choice means letting someone down.

qs.q: Why do Marcus and Alba eliminate the two options that skip an event?
choices: Those options would cost too much money.
The judges would not allow it.
Those options break the rule that both promises must be kept.
Marcus had no interest in soccer or science.
qs.why: The first criterion is keeping both promises, and skipping either event breaks it.

qs.q: Which detail names the obstacle in the final plan?
choices: Marcus emailed the judges.
The coach agreed to start him in the second half.
The fair was across town and the game began forty minutes after the judging ended.
The judges praised the volcano.
qs.why: Distance and a tight time gap stand in the way of the plan, which is why Alba looks for a bus.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses a central idea of the passage?
choices: Luck is the best way to solve a problem.
Sports should always come before school events.
A hard decision gets easier when you list options and judge them with clear standards.
Older siblings should make decisions for younger ones.
qs.why: Marcus lists alternatives, sets criteria, eliminates options, and builds a plan that works.

write.frame: The dilemma was ___, and the top priority was ___, so ___.

study.task: Choose a word from the unit and build two family words with the suffixes -ize, -ation, or -ly. Write one sentence for each family word, and explain how the suffix changed the part of speech.

sentences: Write a sentence about a dilemma a character in a book or movie faced. Say what each option would cost.
Write a sentence that uses both priority and criteria to explain how you would choose a club.
Write a sentence about an obstacle that stands in the way of a goal you have. Name the goal.
Write a sentence that uses strategy and implement to describe a plan being put into action.

They crossed out three of them.
The three failed the cost rule.
combine.model: The team listed five possible plans and eliminated three because they failed the cost rule.

given: Lena felt nervous about the speech.
combine.model: Lena overcame her nervousness about the speech by practicing every night.

discuss: When is it better to deliberate for a long time, and when is it better to decide quickly? Use deliberate in your answer.
Why might two people with different priorities choose different alternatives for the same dilemma?
What makes a set of criteria fair? Give one example.
produce.explain: Explain the difference between deliberate as a verb and deliberate as an adjective. Use a sentence for each meaning.

argue.prompt: Claim: Schools should let students help decide school rules. Take a side and give two reasons, using words from this unit.
argue.frame: I believe that ___ because ___. One alternative would be ___, but the strongest criteria are ___.

constructed.prompt: A friend is invited to two birthday parties on the same afternoon. Write two sentences that explain the dilemma and one alternative the friend could try.
look: shows why each option has a cost
constructed.model: Jordan faces a dilemma because he promised to attend both parties, and each friend would be hurt if he missed theirs. An alternative is to ask one host if he could come for the first hour and leave early.

constructed.prompt: Your class is choosing a field trip. Write a short paragraph that uses criteria, priority, and eliminate to show how you would narrow the list.
look: shows an option being ruled out for a stated reason
constructed.model: Our top priority is a trip that teaches something about science. We set two criteria: it must cost under ten dollars and be reachable by bus. We eliminated the water park because it failed both.

constructed.prompt: Describe a goal, the obstacle in the way, and the strategy a person uses to overcome it.
look: shows a strategy with at least two steps
constructed.model: Nora wanted to finish her book report, but a noisy house was the obstacle. Her strategy was to read at the library after school and write one page each night. She overcame the problem and handed it in early.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten words that name the steps of a hard decision, from the dilemma to the plan to the obstacle. They use the words in a narrative about a double-booked Saturday, work with the suffixes -ize, -ation and -ly, and apply a simple decision method to their own choices.

notes.va.dilemma.n: A dilemma costs something whichever way you go. Students overuse it for any decision; give them a 'good choice vs. good choice' counterexample. Ask what each option costs.
notes.va.alternative.n: Alternative is a noun here: the other option. Students may confuse it with alternate, which means every other one. Use a real example: an alternative route when a road is closed.
notes.va.priority.n: Have students rank five weekend tasks and defend the first. Connect to prioritize and priorities. Note that priority is singular and priorities is plural.
notes.va.obstacle.n: Obstacle is a noun for the thing in the way. Link to the story's obstacle (distance and timing) and ask what the character could do about it. Contrast with a goal.
notes.va.strategy.n: A strategy has steps; a single action is not one. Ask students to name a strategy for reading a hard text. Watch for confusion with strategic (adjective).
notes.va.deliberate.v: Teach the verb first and say it aloud: the last syllable rhymes with gate. Then show the adjective (rhymes with it) as a different word that means on purpose. The confusion is real, so give each a sentence.
notes.va.eliminate.v: Tie to test-taking: eliminating wrong answers. Students often think eliminate means destroy; the idea is rule out or remove. Practice with a four-choice item.
notes.va.implement.v: Implement is to put a plan or rule into action. Mention that implement is also a noun, a tool, so a dictionary may show it first. Ask what a school does to implement a new rule.
notes.va.overcome.v: Overcome is irregular: overcame, overcome. Have students conjugate it. Pair with obstacle: the obstacle is the thing, overcome is what you do to it.
notes.va.criteria.n: Criteria is plural; criterion is singular. Students say 'the criteria is' often. Use a rubric as a concrete example, then have students write two criteria for a good lunch.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'Marcus lists four alternatives. Then he sets criteria, which are the standards for a good solution. The first criterion is keeping both promises. Skipping the tournament fails it, so I eliminate that alternative. The word eliminate means I am ruling it out for a reason I can name.'
discuss: Describe a decision you made carefully. Which of the unit words would you use to tell the story?
How is a priority different from a goal?
misconceptions: An alternative is the same as an alternate.
extend: Choose a historical decision and list the alternatives, criteria, and priority behind it.
Write a problem-solution paragraph that names an obstacle and a strategy to overcome it.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Revisit the decision steps two days later by having students sort the words into 'thinking', 'planning', and 'acting'. At one week, ask them to describe a decision in the news using at least four words. Connect to outcome, cautious, inadequate, and commit from earlier units.

frames: My dilemma is that ___, but also ___.
I will eliminate ___ because it does not meet the criteria of ___.
To overcome the obstacle of ___, our strategy is to ___.
wida.oral: Partner A states a hard choice in one sentence. Partner B names one alternative, one criterion, and which option they would eliminate, using words from the unit.

needsReview: Spanish glosses not reviewed by a native speaker: superar (overcome), deliberar, implementar, criterios, dilema.
Sense boundaries: deliberate taught as a verb with the adjective as a second sense; implement as a verb only (the noun tool sense is named only in the teacher note); alternative as a noun only.
Pronunciation respellings for deliberate (verb), implement (verb) and criteria follow common US dictionary pronunciations; confirm with a dictionary.
